title: Hackers Probed Europe's Fridge Systems for 10 Days Before Attacks
excerpt: Lupovis says more than 276 probing attempts preceded the November 2-3 attacks on Danfoss refrigeration controllers in nine countries — but who was behind them remains unestablished.
body:
• Refrigeration systems in supermarkets across nine European countries, and several blood banks in France, were attacked on November 2 and 3, according to Euronews.
  • Cybersecurity firm Lupovis says it recorded more than 276 probing attempts from 91 threat actors between October 20 and 30, peaking on October 26, before the attacks.
  • Hackers exploited Danfoss AK-SM refrigeration controllers, putting units into defrost and in some cases raising temperatures to 50 degrees Celsius; stores threw away spoiled produce.
  • Attribution is not established: Lupovis says hosting previously used by Russian groups was involved and that a state actor fits its assessment, while other experts caution the attackers could have been anyone and no one has claimed responsibility.

Hackers probed internet-connected refrigeration systems across Europe in the days before a wave of attacks disrupted supermarkets and blood banks, cybersecurity researchers told Euronews. Refrigeration systems in supermarkets across nine European countries, as well as several blood banks in France, were attacked on November 2 and 3.

Hackers exploited weak cybersecurity and vulnerabilities in manufacturer Danfoss's AK-SM refrigeration system manager to put fridges and freezers on defrost settings, in some cases setting temperatures as high as 50 degrees Celsius, Euronews reported. The incidents forced many grocery stores to throw away spoiled produce.

Ten days of probing before the attacks

For cybersecurity firm Lupovis, the signs point to a coordinated operation potentially involving a state actor, preceded by days of probing. The company said it observed more than 276 attempts coming from 91 different threat actors matching specific components of Danfoss controllers during a 10-day period, with activity peaking on October 26 before coming to a halt at the end of the month.

"Between the 20th and 30th of October, what we saw was a wave of what we call reconnaissance."

— Xavier Bellekens, CEO of Lupovis, to Euronews Next

Lupovis detected the activity through honeypots — systems that replicate clients' online systems, are equipped with sensors, and are deliberately exposed so the firm can track how they are accessed and exploited, Euronews reported. Bellekens told Euronews the adversaries were trying default passwords and a couple of vulnerabilities during the peak.

Who did it? The sources do not agree on an answer

Lupovis traced what it describes as digital breadcrumbs and found that so-called bulletproof hosting was used — hosting designed to resist takedown requests and law enforcement intervention. Bellekens said some of that hosting had been used by Russian groups in the past. The company is clear, Euronews reported, that server location does not establish the nationality of the people using it, so it cannot say for sure that Russia was behind the attacks. Bellekens said Lupovis sensors in South America, Africa, North America and Asia did not record the same activity — only sensors in Europe did — and that coordinating attacks within about 24 hours pointed, in his assessment, to a well-planned operation rather than a lone amateur.

Other experts quoted by Euronews urged caution. George Nott, technology editor at The Grocer, said it was still unclear who was behind the attack or what they hoped to achieve, and that with no ransom demand or claim of responsibility, it could have been anyone from a state-sponsored actor to teenagers. A separate incident review by Rescana, summarising the November 2 wave, likewise recorded that no group had been named, no one had claimed responsibility, and Reuters was unable to establish who was behind those attacks or whether they were linked to an earlier October wave in France.

Agencies also differed in language. Belgium, Luxembourg, Italy, Portugal and Estonia called the incidents a cyberattack, while Sweden and Ireland referred to a cyber incident, and the European Union's Agency for Cybersecurity stopped short of explicitly calling them a cyberattack, according to Euronews.

How the systems were reached

The controller boxes were connected to the internet so refrigeration units could be managed remotely, Bellekens told Euronews. He said many systems could have been better protected on virtual private networks rather than exposed directly to the internet, and that a VPN would have entirely mitigated the risk in his assessment. Many systems were reportedly accessible using factory-default credentials, such as username "Supervisor" and password "12345", Euronews reported. Nott said attackers found login pages on the open internet and exploited already patched vulnerabilities and weak passwords, rather than highly advanced technology.

France's cyber agency guidance, summarised by Rescana from the CERT-FR alert, advises removing refrigeration controllers from public internet exposure, restoring remote access only through a secure VPN or protected network, changing default passwords, and patching or replacing end-of-life units.

What could be targeted next

The concern, experts told Euronews, is the wider class of small internet-connected controllers. Nott warned that heating, ventilation and air conditioning systems, electronic shelf labels and floor cleaning robots in supermarkets could present similar vulnerabilities if remote access is not properly secured and software is not patched. Kumar Sokka, CEO of Acre Security, told Euronews the same kind of controller also runs doors, access-control readers, cameras, alarms, lighting and heating and ventilation in many modern buildings, and that logistics, healthcare, manufacturing and data centres could be exposed where connected equipment was introduced without sufficient oversight.

Gianni Cuozzo, founder and CEO of Italian cybersecurity firm Exein, told Euronews that AI is collapsing the time between finding a vulnerability and turning it into a working attack, and listed refrigeration, building controls, industrial equipment, healthcare systems, data centres and parts of energy and transport infrastructure among the systems he would worry about most.
